Yes, you need tamper-resistant packaging for your mouthwash sold on open drugstore shelves because the product is a cosmetic liquid oral hygiene product accessible to the public while held for sale [2].  

The requirement applies if the mouthwash is packaged for retail sale and is accessible to the public during retail display; the package must have an indicator or barrier to entry that provides visible evidence of tampering if breached or missing, and this feature must be distinctive by design—meaning it cannot be duplicated with commonly available materials or processes—and must remain intact when handled in a reasonable manner during manufacture, distribution, and retail display [2].  

A prominent labeling statement is required on each retail package (except aerosol products) that alerts consumers to the specific tamper-resistant feature of the package, and this statement must remain visible even if the tamper-resistant feature is breached or missing. If the tamper-resistant feature uses an identifying characteristic (e.g., a pattern, name, logo), that characteristic must be referenced in the labeling statement [3].  

The tamper-resistant packaging requirement is effective on February 7, 1983 for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for vaginal tablets, and is effective on May 5, 1983 for vaginal tablets; the full requirements, including a distinctive indicator by design and labeling statement, are effective on May 5, 1983 for all affected cosmetic products, with the specific reference to identifying characteristics becoming effective on February 6, 1984 [10][12]. The requirement is also effective on or after February 6, 1984 for products held for sale on or after that date [13].  

The requirement does not apply to aerosol products, which are defined as those depending on liquefied or compressed gas to expel contents [2].  

An exemption from the packaging and labeling requirements may be requested through a citizen petition under §700.25(d), which must include the name of the product, reasons that compliance is unnecessary or unachievable, and other information justifying an exemption [5][6][7].  

The requirement applies to all cosmetic liquid oral hygiene products accessible to the public while held for sale; it does not apply to products not accessible to the public during retail display [2].
